transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-15 15:00 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Samira Khan, Diego Rivera (Redwood); Maya Patel, Ethan Ross, Priya Nair, Liam Chen (Aurelia Labs)

Summary: quick scoping call to lock down latency SLOs and measurement plan for Aurelia Labs POC. Notes have some transcription noise.

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Maya: Hi, Maya here, CTO.
[00:08] Ethan: Ethan, ML eng.
[00:10] Priya: Priya infra.
[00:12] Liam: Liam product.
[00:15] Samira: Great. Diego from SE on my side as well. Purpose today is to align on TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, workload sizing and how we'll measure during the POC.

[02:05] Diego: Quick definitions so we're on the same page — TTFT is time to first token, that's the latency the user feels for initial response. TPOT in our notes stands for time per output token which is basically throughput after the first token. Some teams use tokens/sec or ms/token, same idea.

[04:20] Maya: For our app we care both about initial latency because doctors need a quick answer, and throughput because we batch lots of transcripts overnight.

[05:10] Ethan: To give you context our typical prompt length is 120–300 tokens, distribution attached later. Peak concurrent requests hit around 60–80 users during clinic hours, but bulk batch jobs run at 2k concurrent workers in a different flow.

[06:02] Diego: Helpful. For the POC we suggest separating interactive SLOs and batch SLOs. Interactive: aim for TTFT p95 <= 200 ms, p99 <= 450 ms for a mid-size base model with KV cache warmed. Batch: target TPOT equivalent — e.g., sustained throughput of X tokens/sec per GPU and time-per-token p95 <= 40 ms for tail tokens, but we can express as throughput too.

[07:10] Priya: Those numbers feel optimistic; our infra historically sees 300–500 ms 95th for small models. Also encryption/KMS calls might add latency.

[07:40] Samira: Good point — KMS hops matter. For private deploys we measure KMS latency in the loop and can factor that in. For hosted/dedicated we also test with and without external KMS to establish delta.

[09:00] Ethan: Can you walk through how you measure TTFT? Is it from request arrival to first byte at the client?

[09:18] Diego: We measure server-side time-to-first-token at the API gateway and at the model router — client measurements are dependent on network. So metric names we'll collect: api_ttft_server_ms, model_send_queue_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate, token_gen_ms, tokens_per_sec, gpu_util_pct, batch_size. We'll capture p50/p90/p95/p99.

[11:22] Liam: For SLO targets we need both absolute numbers and relative improvement vs current baseline.

[12:05] Samira: Agreed. Proposed initial SLOs for the POC (interact): TTFT p95 = 250 ms (goal 200 ms), TTFT p99 = 500 ms. TPOT (steady token phase) p95 = 30–50 ms per token depending on model size; we'll express batch throughput as tokens/sec with target based on your target concurrency.

[13:40] Maya: Let's be explicit: for our interactive clinical assistant we want p95 < 300 ms and p99 < 600 ms as acceptance for the pilot, but we'd like Redwood to show path to 200/400.

[14:12] Diego: Noted. We'll run two benchmark profiles: interactive profile (arrival pattern like Poisson, concurrency 10–100, prompt length distribution you give) and batch profile (sustained high qps with large token outputs). We'll run both cold runs and warmed cache runs.

[16:00] Ethan: What about batching and continuous batching? Our traffic is spiky so latency SLOs need to account for batching-induced tail.

[16:25] Diego: We'll parameterize batch size and max latency budgets. Our harness can simulate dynamic batching thresholds, and we can pin batch sizes to see impact on TTFT and tokens/sec. Also KV cache should dramatically reduce TTFT for repeated prefixes.

[18:00] Priya: For private deployment, network egress and VPC peering add 10–50 ms. We'll need runbook notes for isolating network impact.

[19:10] Samira: We'll include phased measurement: 1) synthetic benchmarks in Redwood lab (controlled), 2) customer-hosted synthetic tests (to account for KMS/VPC), 3) production shadowing with sampling, 4) sustained soak test.

[20:40] Liam: What tools will you use for synthetic load?

[20:50] Diego: Our standard is a combination: Locust for request patterns, a custom tokens-aware generator to measure TPOT, and internal harness that collects per-token timing from runtime. We can provide JMX-exported metrics or push to your Prometheus during the POC.

[22:30] Ethan: We need to capture cold-start vs warm-start percentiles separately. Also measure queueing delay when concurrency exceeds available slots.

[23:12] Diego: Yes — cold start and warm start labels will be separate metrics. We'll do warm runs after a warm-up period and report both. For queueing we'll record queue_time_ms and rejection_rate.

[25:00] Maya: Success criteria: acceptable interactive experience for clinicians and bounded batch window for nightly jobs. If p95/p99 exceed thresholds by >20% across two runs, that's a fail and we revisit config.

[26:10] Samira: We'll also include qualitative evals: correctness/regression tests on a small eval set to ensure quantization or performance tweaks don't degrade response quality. Redwood Optimize will run recommendations but we will validate outputs.

[28:00] Ethan: On model choices — are you recommending quantized models for the POC?

[28:20] Diego: We'll propose two model variants: quantized (8-bit / 4-bit) for cost/throughput and FP16 baseline. We'll measure quality/regressions on your eval prompts. If quantization causes regressions we'll flag and tune.

[30:00] Priya: For measurement windows, how long will each benchmark run be?

[30:12] Diego: Typical approach: short ramp (5–10m), steady-state (15–30m) for percentile stability, then cooldown. For soak tests we do 2–4 hour runs overnight. We'll pick durations with you.

[32:05] Maya: We need reporting format. A single spreadsheet with baseline, test configs, and percentile tables is ideal.

[32:30] Samira: We'll send a baseline benchmark spreadsheet. It will include columns: test_id, model, quantization, prompt_set, concurrency, arrival_pattern, batch_size, TTFT_p50/p95/p99, TPOT_p50/p95/p99, tokens_per_sec, gpu_util, kv_cache_hit_rate, notes.

[34:45] Diego: Measurement plan summary: collect API TTFT, model-side TTFT, per-token ms, tokens/sec, GPU util, queue_time, KV cache hit rates, KMS latency when present. We'll compare server-side vs client-side when possible.

[36:10] Ethan: For recording we need dashboards; can Redwood push to our Prometheus or do you provide a Grafana snapshot?

[36:28] Samira: Both possible. We'll push Prometheus metrics and provide dashboard templates in Redwood Console. If you want hosted dashboard access we can grant read-only.

[38:00] Liam: Timelines — when can the initial benchmarks run?

[38:10] Samira: If we get your prompt corpus and token distribution by 2026-08-19, Redwood can run lab benchmarks on 2026-08-20–21 and share results 2026-08-22. Then customer-hosted runs and shadowing start the week of 2026-08-24.

[39:20] Maya: That timeline works. Also security review is a gating item for private deployment. We'll need SOC2/ISO docs and KMS integration notes.

[40:00] Samira: We'll attach security package and network runbook.

[40:30] Diego: A few engineering clarifications for Ethan/Priya: please confirm target concurrency for interactive (10/50/100) and batch concurrency windows for nightly. Also confirm whether you want strict hard SLOs or graduated accepted ranges during pilot.

[41:10] Ethan: We'll provide a target matrix (interactive 25 p95 target 300 ms, p99 600 ms; batch target is X tokens/sec per GPU) — exact values by 2026-08-19.

[42:00] Priya: On the private deployment side we'll need a baseline network latency test to Redwood endpoints to understand impact. We'll run iperf and share.

[43:00] Diego: Great. We'll include network impact as a delta in the benchmark spreadsheet.

[45:10] Samira: Recap of accepted initial SLOs: Aurelia acceptance for pilot: interactive TTFT p95 < 300 ms, p99 < 600 ms. Redwood goal: show path to TTFT p95 <= 200 ms and p99 <= 450 ms with tuning. Batch: measure tokens/sec and make sure nightly jobs complete within the current SLA window — we'll set a numeric target once we see your token distribution.

[47:20] Liam: Who owns the pilot run coordination?

[47:28] Samira: Samira and Diego will coordinate on Redwood side; Ethan and Priya will coordinate on Aurelia side.

[48:00] Maya: Any risks you foresee?

[48:10] Diego: Main risks: KMS-induced tail, VPC peering latency, cold-starts for scale-to-zero, and model quality regressions post-quantization. We'll enumerate mitigations in the runbook.

[50:00] Ethan: For instrumentation, please include trace IDs so we can correlate requests end-to-end.

[50:18] Diego: Yes, we'll add tracing and correlation ids.

[51:40] Samira: Next steps quick list: we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet, Redwood security package and dashboard templates; Aurelia sends prompt corpus, token distribution, network latency data, and confirm SLO matrix. Schedule pilot kickoff for 2026-08-24.

[54:00] Maya: Thanks everyone.

[54:05] Samira: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript. Note: transcript contains minor transcription noise (names sometimes shortened, punctuation inconsistent).
